speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-121, to authorize the provision of moneys to meet certain capital expenditures of the Canadian National Railways system for the period from the 1st day of July, 1961 to the 30th day of June, 1962 and to authorize the guarantee by Her Majesty of certain securities to be issued by the Canadian National Railway Company.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I think there is probably little that I can usefully say concerning this measure on this motion for second reading. The matter was considered in committee at the resolution stage on July 6, and I think the necessary explanations were given at that time.
Canadian National Railways
Bill No. C-121 follows precisely the terms of the resolution. That resolution was in what has become something of a standard form. It is the same form as was used last year, with the addition of one clause which becomes necessary this year for special reasons which I explained at the committee stage. Since the resolution was reported and the bill given first reading the report of the sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping owned and controlled by the government was tabled in the house yesterday and is available to all hon. members.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister has made another short statement in connection with the second reading of this bill, but neither he nor the Minister of Transport has answered the questions which we put to them at the resolution stage. At that time we made it quite clear that we would object strenuously to the passage of this measure until we knew who the new directors of the Canadian National Railways were going to be and what was the status and position of the president.
After all, sir, the bill to increase the number of directors of the C.N.R. from seven to 12 was passed many weeks ago, and I think the house is entitled to know, by virtue of the doctrine enunciated by the Prime Minister in another debate yesterday, who these directors are going to be, when parliament is being asked to authorize the expenditure of vast sums of money by the Canadian National Railways. Notwithstanding the statement made by the Minister of Finance, no information has been given to us in that regard.
There was another complaint made from this side of the house. It had to do with the custom and practice concerning this refinancing bill for the C.N.R., namely that it should not have been introduced until the report of the committee on railways, air lines and shipping had been made. When the resolution was introduced that report had not been made. It has now been tabled. Again I repeat, this only points up the disorder and the delay on the part of the government in organizing the business of the house. The business of the house with reference to committees has been so badly organized that it was not possible for this important committee to meet until the dying days of the session, whereas the custom has been over the years for the committee dealing with the annual reports of the C.N.R. and T.C.A. to meet much earlier. As I indicated on a previous occasion, the committee has met in March and April but rarely, in my recollection, has that committee met as late as June, save and except when the parliamentary session was late in beginning its deliberations. I shall come tc that matter again at a later stage.

Canadian National Railways
The bill which is now before us and for which second reading is sought seeks to authorize the Canadian National Railways to meet certain expenditures for the period January 1, 1961 to June 30, 1962; next, to authorize the guarantee by Her Majesty of certain securities issued by the Canadian National Railways. That provision was broken down into six parts by the minister when he introduced the resolution. I will not go into all of those, but I should like to make a general reference to them.
The first purpose sought by this measure is to authorize the C.N.R. to incur capital expenditures not exceeding $179 million, roughly speaking, during the calendar year 1961; next, to authorize the company to make prior to July 1, 1962 such capital expenditures as may be necessary to discharge obligations incurred under the 1961 act. Third, the purpose to be served by the bill is to authorize the railways to enter into contracts prior to July 1, 1962 for new equipment.
There are also three other provisions in the resolution which have been referred to by the minister. They have to do with the capital revision of the Canadian National Railways. They have to do more particularly with extending provisions which were contained in enactments recommended by the previous royal commission on transportation way back in 1950, the Turgeon commission. They deal first with the intention on the part of the government to proceed with the re-examination and revision of the capital structure of the railway company prior to December 31, 1961. I should like to quote the minister's words, which are to be found at page 7640 of Hansard of July 6, 1961:
However, since the complete report of the royal commission on transportation has not yet been received it was considered advisable to make provision in the 1961 act for a one-year extension of the present capital structure.
The minister went on to say:
As the president of the C.N.R. indicated in the recent hearings before the sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping, the capital structure is at present under study. This review will be continued in the light of the complete report of the royal commission once it has been received.
The report of the committee on railways, air lines and shipping, which was tabled yesterday by the vice-chairman of that committee, contains one passage which I think should be brought to the attention of the house in this respect. It is the one entitled "Deficits", and it reads as follows:
The committee noted with concern Mr. Gordon's evidence to the effect that consideration was given to asking the government of Canada to take over from $700 million to $900 million of the railways debt structure.
This proposal has two unusual aspects: (1) the royal commission of 1950 dealt at length with debt


problems of the C.N.R., recommending an alleviation which was carried out in 1952; (2) a most recent royal commission has completed its hearings without any evidence by the C.N.R. on the need for another debt revision. In the light of this, the committee suggests that the government examine such a proposition with great care.
There seems to be a difference between the statement made by the minister on the resolution and the recommendation made by the committee, and I wonder if the minister when he closes the debate would deal with this aspect of the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. gentleman would be good enough to enlarge on that point so I might follow him more clearly. I should be glad to comment on it if I can, but I am not too clear as to where he finds any difference.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I shall be glad to do so as I go along. I am a member of this committee, but because of the debates on other matters which took place in this house I did not attend the meetings at which this report was prepared and drafted. Incidentally, in passing, I think those members who sit on this side of the house would wish to extend to the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) our commendation for the manner in which he carried on as chairman of that committee. Not only did he deal objectively with a committee which might well have brought in recommendations which could have caused serious concern to the national railways, but he dealt with the affairs of the committee in an orderly and efficient manner.
I should like also to say a word of felicitation to the vice-chairman, the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Smith) who, when the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe unfortunately fell ill, carried on, particularly with the meeting having to do with the report. I am sure the members on this side of the house would wish me to extend to him our commendation. I should also like to say to the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe that we hope he will be quickly and completely restored to health.
Having said that, I come to the matter of the revision of the capital structure of the Canadian National Railways. The house will remember that in 1951 the Turgeon royal commission made certain recommendations, most of which were afterwards adopted by the government of the day, dealing with the capital structure of that company. These recommendations may be found at page 196 of the report and I have no intention of reading them, because they are lengthy. They can be seen by anyone who is interested. The Canadian National Railways had asked for these recommendations, or at least had made

representations directed towards these recommendations, and the government saw fit to implement them.
I gather from the statements which the minister made during consideration of this matter on July 6 that the revision of the Canadian National Railways capital structure was under consideration by the government at the suggestion of the C.N.R. and, further, that the matter was also under consideration by the royal commission on transportation. Canadian National Railways

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope I can get through my remarks without points of order such as those that have been flying around here recently. The railways, air lines and shipping committee report has been tabled, and this gives us an opportunity to both use the evidence that was presented before that committee and to speak with more information with regard to this measure.
Let me say that we support the measure. We think it is a routine financial measure, and we support it. There are a considerable number of comments, however, I should like to make.
The report that was tabled yesterday took cognizance of a number of points that came up. First, there was a mild-at least it is my interpretation-slap on the wrist of the president for his attack in the committee on members of parliament. Second, there were some general remarks about the financial position of the Canadian National, and there was critical comment about the way in which Canadian National Railways got into trucking operations. There were some suggestions with regard to the United States operations of the C.N.R.; there was a paragraph on pensions and a suggestion how that particular problem should be handled, and there was a brief paragraph relating to the morale of the employees.
The position of the C.C.F. party with regard to the Canadian National Railways might be worth stating again, since as our party spokesman in the house on the C.N.R. I have read and heard the accusation in certain places that I have been out to chop down or destroy the Canadian National Railways. We support the Canadian National Railways as a public institution, and will go on supporting it. I have here G. R. Stevens' book "Canadian National Railways". In the introduction to this book there is a brief paragraph that I think covers the great value of the C.N.R. and all railways in Canada. It says:
The economic value of a railway to the community is determined not by the railway's income account and balance sheet, but by the social dividends the community receives from the reduced cost of transportation. The primary dividend is the money saved by using rail transport rather than any other kind. In the middle of the last century the difference in cost was astounding, at least twenty times that of providing railway service. Even in these days of motor vehicles, this dividend is still a vital force in our economy; money that is saved for the community by the use of rail transport is at least three times the total expenses of the railways, including interest on capital. Not infrequently the income account and balance sheet of railways indicate something less than financial success; but they scarcely reveal the impact of railways on the economy of the country.


We know there is a great necessity for the Canadian National Railways. In the part of the country which I represent there is a tremendous amount of C.N.R. mileage. That mileage is not only an integral part of the whole economy of our region, but it is part of that bridge that links the west and the east together. The Canadian National Railways as a crown corporation of the 1960's is the kind of organization that we support. We only expect from that organization that it is run on the best possible basis in terms of both business efficiency and public service. When those two factors come into contradiction-that is, efficiency and public service-then we believe it is the responsibility of the government which owns the corporation to indicate just how we are going to deal with the problem.
One issue that always comes up in connection with the Canadian National Railways, and it has been brought to the fore by the Financial Post recently, is whether we are ready in Canada for an amalgamation or what is sometimes called a rationalization of the two major class 1 railways. Our party position in regard to this matter is that it is a subject that is so pertinent and relevant at the present time that I want to make it perfectly clear that if the matter is to be studied, we feel it should be studied with the emphasis on the Canadian National Railways taking over the railway lines of the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Mr. Speaker, I now want to talk in much greater detail about the appearance of the president of the Canadian National Railways before the committee, because as an individual member of parliament I was involved in a way that was in some ways unique so far as members of the committee were concerned. I should like to make one point in contradistinction to what has been said by the hon. member for Laurier. Mr. Gordon had his period, if one wants to call it that, in court before the shareholders, if one wants to call them that. Mr. Gordon is not in a similar position to Mr. Coyne in this regard at all. It would seem to me that with regard to the argument that public servants are frightened or scared at the present time, the hon. member for Laurier may be able to make that an issue in certain areas, but I believe that in the area of the president of the Canadian National Railways this does not apply.
I would go along with the hon. member to a degree, that we need to know whether the president of the Canadian National Railways is going to be reappointed. I think he knows our views on whether or not this should happen. But I feel, as an individual trying to judge the situation, that it is perhaps one of

the best things possible for the Canadian National Railways at the present time to keep Mr. Gordon in some kind of suspension, because I think it will result in a better job of management of the Canadian National Railways. I would not advocate it as a permanent feature.
The performance of the president of the Canadian National Railways before the committee was to quite an extent in marked contrast to his previous appearances. If I could make some kind of a simile or metaphor it would be that this time it was as though he was appearing at a cocktail party rather than in the locker room. He was much milder and much more informative than ever before. I think all hon. members who sat on this committee in other years will agree that in the past Mr. Gordon did not give the impression of having a team working with him. He dominated all the evidence; he gave almost all the evidence, and we had to search very far to find evidence from other people who supported him in his so-called management team.
This year we had many more people in the committee in support of the president of the Canadian National Railways. It was quite apparent that they were being encouraged to give more evidence, to fill in more background and so give the members of the committee much more information. They had this information at their fingertips for us. To me this was a victory in the sense that this year we got both a more informative presentation and a wider presentation from the president of the Canadian National Railways. It seems to me this change is all for the good, and I certainly had the impression that the members of the committee were impressed with the fact that we received more information.
I should like to deal with the fact that during the committee hearings we were all aware that Mr. Gordon's position had been attacked in this house. I suggested, and other members of the committee also suggested, that he be given a full opportunity to state his case. He did so, on a number of aspects of the work, and he spoke particularly in relation to charges of members of parliament relating to him. I wish to touch on a number of these, Mr. Speaker, because it seems to me they affect all members of the committee and all hon. members of the house.
One of the things Mr. Gordon said was that McCarthy-like tactics had been introduced. I should like to make this point, that McCarthy-like tactics usually relate to indicating that someone is a subversive. I received a letter yesterday from somebody by the name of Pat Walsh suggesting that I am a subversive
Canadian National Railways because I sent letters to hon. members of the house advertising a nuclear radiation hazards meeting. This, it seems to me, is a McCarthy-like tactic.
Mr. Gordon felt he had been treated with McCarthy-like tactics. I do not know of any hon. member of this house who is critical of Mr. Gordon in the sense of thinking he is a subversive. I do not believe Mr. Gordon is a communist. I am certain he is not. I am certain he is not even a C.C.F.'er. I do not know what his politics are. I suspect them, but I do not think it has anything to do with the job he does. If Mr. Gordon is a Liberal, I do not think that is a factor which is at all relevant to the job he may do as president of the Canadian National Railways. It seems to me this was a most unfair, gratuitous way to come back at criticism, to suggest that people who criticize him were using McCarthy-like tactics. It seems to me his politics were never called into question at any time.
I now wish to deal with the matter of Mr. Gordon being called arrogant, haughty and dictatorial. I went to the trouble of reading what I had said about Mr. Gordon in the House of Commons. I have never at any time called him arrogant, dictatorial or haughty, as has been suggested. The strongest words I have ever used in this house about Mr. Gordon were that he was a man of brutal candour. But what I did suggest-and this seems to have caused a reaction on the part of Mr. Gordon-was that he should be fired. Perhaps this is a vicious criticism; but surely, Mr. Speaker, when you reach the stage that you think someone who has had 12 years to do a job is not doing it very well, there is nothing wrong in getting up and quite fairly saying that you think the man should be fired.
Apparently Mr. Gordon felt I was the central figure in the attacks upon him, because he came to the committee well prepared, I think, to take several rounds out of me. I want to comment upon a couple of these; because while I will not say that Mr. Gordon was untruthful in a couple of his charges, it does seem to me that he did not give all the factors in the situation. I should like to point out to hon. members

I hate to bring up this individual matter-that I was accused in this committee of being a lawbreaker, which is a fairly serious charge; of being a braggart, which is more of a political charge than a serious charge. I was accused of conniving at thievery, and of being a smearer. I should just like to analyse the charge of lawbreaking first, because to me this is typical of the inability of the president of the Canadian National Railways to react to criticism.

Canadian National Railways
It all arose from a statement made by the president in the committee last year. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River brought up a very difficult situation which had developed in a community in his constituency, one which was causing a great deal of dislocation. We were given, I understood, an undertaking by Mr. Gordon that if such a situation threatened to develop again as a result of changes in the railway which were really going to dislocate a community, he would see that the community concerned was informed well ahead of time. Well, last year a group of men representing several railway communities came down here and showed that they had nine days' notice of the introduction of a form of service which would vitally and drastically affect the population and the well being of one community in my constituency and one community in the constituency of the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Godin). The hon. member for Nickel Belt and I talked the matter over with these men and asked them what could be done. They had been to the Minister of Transport. Their general chairman had been to see the management, and the management intended to go ahead with its plans.

speechtext: You talked it over with me, too.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
No doubt. The men were in a great deal of distress over this, and they kept insisting that they just could not go through with this change in service which meant running through two divisions. They felt that from the point of view of safety it was unsound, and having regard to their own personal positions they did not have time to straighten out their affairs in these communities. They felt so strongly about this that I said "Well, what can you do? What can you do if you have got to accept this?" And they said "We just will not go to work". I said, "Well, you cannot pull a wildcat strike". The general chairman there said "If they pull a wildcat strike they will go to jail". At that time I noted these words very well. I said "If you feel so strongly about it you should be prepared to go to jail. After all, I do not think there is any greater test of your feelings about something than whether you are prepared to go to jail about it".
This, apparently, is the lawbreaking that I did. This is the advice which Mr. Gordon feels is lawbreaking. Well, what happened as a result of the fact that the men announced that they were going to pull themselves out of service was that the railway postponed for a short while putting its plan into operation and accepted the compromise which the men suggested. Here is the irony. Mr. Gordon

accused me of costing the C.N.R. money because of my role in this matter. He accused me of lawbreaking. I was up in those communities last week in order to get all the particulars of the situation and talk it over with the men. They do not think I am a lawbreaker. They do not think I cost the C.N.R. any money. As a matter of fact they pointed out to me that right in the bulletin books of the divisional point at Capreol there was a letter from the management of the C.N.R. congratulating them on the wonderful way this service, as it had been introduced according to their compromise, was going. The letter said they were making better time and giving better service than other places on the Canadian National Railways system. Now, the management of the C.N.R. does not go to those lengths to compliment its employees if something is not working well, and in the light of this fact I think Mr. Gordon's charge that I had cost the railway a great deal of money and am a lawbreaker was nonsensical.
There is one other aspect of this which is much more important to me than to anyone else. Mr. Gordon accused me of conniving at thievery. I think all members are aware that they get communications from people in many diverse forms. During the committee hearings I received long distance telephone calls; visitors came to my office; I received several hundred letters. A great deal of information comes to us, and in almost every aspect of our work a great deal of this information comes to us in confidence. I had been presented by a person, who at one time had a connection with the trucking operations of the Canadian National Railways, with a statement regarding the performance of these operations in the year 1960. Because this document was given to me in confidence I had no intention of revealing the source, and I was not using the document in any other way except that I just kept asking the president of the C.N.R. whether it was not true that his truck lines lost money in 1960. I suggested an estimated figure.
Well, as you probably know, Mr. Speaker, he wanted to know where I was getting this information, and when I suggested that I had this paper here it wound up on the table. We had a little bit of a wrestling match over it, and that document became part of the record. Mr. Gordon identified the document as a document stolen from the files of the Canadian National Railways. I doubt very much whether it was a stolen document in any very real sense in relation to the way in which I got it. I still feel that I am privy in not revealing the name of the person who gave it to me. Anyway, the document was recognized as part of the record.

Now I should just like to suggest to hon. members that if one is going to be informed with regard to the many matters which arise, one must accept, with a certain critical approach, the various people who come to one and give information in confidence. If this led me to being in possession of what was said to be a stolen document, I have no support or flattery to put forward to the person who provided this to me, but I take strenuous exception to the suggestion that I either connived in obtaining a stolen document or, knowing that it was stolen, used it in any vicious or nasty way.
There is one other criticism which the president made. He said he did not feel that the head of a $3| billion corporation should have to stand the kind of criticism that he received in the House of Commons from members of parliament. I asked him to make a statement in this particular regard because I felt he should have his day in court, as one says. He took off, and the committee has noted that he did and questioned his wisdom and propriety in doing so.
It seems to me, despite the talk the hon. member for Laurier gave about the treatment of civil servants and so on, that it is sometimes difficult for civil servants and public servants to recognize that we as members of parliament have a certain responsibility. Although I disagreed with the hon. member who succeeded the late secretary of state for external affairs in some of the remarks he made about Mr. Gordon, what was there wrong about his standing up here in his place, to which he has been elected, and giving his opinion in this respect? I see nothing wrong with it; and the charge that this has undermined the morale of the Canadian National Railways by calling the management into question is a substantial charge, but I wonder if we should accept it. Each of us, through our constituents and the public organizations which work in our constituencies, becomes aware of certain opinions, certain views; we come to certain conclusions about the work of government organizations. I cannot see anything wrong in this particular case with a responsible member getting up in the house and stating what he thinks about how a government organization is run, and expressing his opinions about the individuals who run it.
One of the unfortunate things in regard to the appearance of Mr. Gordon before the committee-this has nothing to do with him personally-occurred because of the rather juvenile attitude taken by many members of the press. I was telephoned on at least five occasions one day by a newspaperman who was attempting to determine my height, chesl
Canadian National Railways measurement and so on apparently in an effort to write a story comparing me in size with Mr. Gordon, almost as though there was to be some kind of a Patterson-Johann-son bout.

speechtext: A bout of overweights, not heavyweights.

speechtext:
The hon. member may be right, that this was a bout of overweights, but I suggest it is this kind of wrong association in respect to committee meetings which causes the kind of criticism which we certainly do not deserve.
I should like to make one final point in regard to the personal charges against the president of the C.N.R. by myself. I reiterate that all my questions directed to the president of the C.N.R. were direct questions and not criticisms. The only criticism I made in the house was that he should be fired and that he possessed a certain brutal candour. If the president of the Canadian National Railways cannot stand up to that type of criticism that is all the more reason why he should go.
Mr. Speaker, I should like at this point to say something about what I think are Mr. Gordon's failures as president of the Canadian National Railways. The irony of the situation is that we have a banker as head of the railway. He is a man who was going to bring to the railroad a great understanding of financial matters, such as bonds, capital, and so on. This is a man who is a great financier with great experience, particularly during the last war; and who did, as we have been told, a magnificent job in respect to one aspect of government operations. He has been head of the railway for 12 years and now comes up with a $900 million bombshell. It apparently has taken him almost 12 years to discover that the financial picture of this railway does not look good because there should be a shift in bookkeeping entries of $900 million from the debt structure to the government of Canada. He suggests that once that has been accomplished he will be able to present a very good financial picture.
As the hon. member for Acadia said, I am a simple boy from the bush, and this does not quite make sense to me. He was referring to this great banker spending 12 years with the railway and then coming up with $900 million bookkeeping shift to put the financial picture of the Canadian National Railways in a wonderful light. That is the capital revision that the Minister of Finance is going to have to consider.
The point I should like to make to the hon. member for Laurier is that the reason the committee said in its recommendations that

Canadian National Railways in the light of this suggestion the government should examine the proposition with great care is that we have already had two large capital revisions in the Canadian National Railways. We have had a royal commission which sat for a year and a half, with evidence piled quite high, at which the C.N.R. was well represented by a capable solicitor, and on some occasions more than one; yet during all that time there was not one word said by any representative of the Canadian National Railways regarding this $900 million shift. As a matter of fact we have not as yet received a complete report from that commission, although we have the first volume. It seems to me that this royal commission had the responsibility of studying the whole railway transportation picture, yet Mr. Gordon did not find it necessary to mention this $700 million to $1,200 million difficulty at any time during its sittings.
Mr. Gordon, the man who, as I have said, was a banker with some experience and who has now been in charge of the railway for 12 years, at this late date has decided that the explanation for the Canadian National Railways deficit lies in a bookkeeping shift. I suggest there has been irresponsibility here in this regard, because the royal commission has suggested that subsidies be paid in the amount of $100 million per year. What is the relationship between those subsidies and the fact that if Mr. Gordon is successful in his suggestion something between $40 million and $50 million of the C.N.R. deficit will disappear? Surely in that event there will be created a completely different picture. Perhaps if we allow this bookkeeping change we will not need to adopt the royal commission's recommendations as to subsidies. I do not know the answer, but suggest that because Mr. Gordon has only at this stage come to this conclusion, this is a failure on his part.
One other point I should like to touch upon has regard to the tremendous management reorganization of the Canadian National Railways. By this change completely new areas and regions will be created. The results of this change may be excellent and responsive to the needs, but it is coming only now after an 11 or 12 year occupancy of the president's position by Mr. Gordon. This change is being made, as the president himself admitted, without adequate preparation and information, particularly in regard to employees, with the result that morale has been demoralized. Employees have not been adequately informed or prepared in respect to this proposed change. Mr. Gordon himself seems to oscillate between the position of not informing the employees, because they just


get their backs up and get excited, and working out better public relations.
Mr. Gordon has already begun to use his public relations resources. Not long ago on his return to Montreal, according to the press, he was greeted by a crowd of 800 employees. Hon. members will remember the picture of him coming through the door being greeted by this crowd of 800 employees. I received a letter from an individual who was in that crowd, informing me that he had received notice from his supervisor to be in attendance at this spontaneous welcome. As a consequence of this information I asked that individual how big the crowd was, and received information that it was not more than about 300. I do not know which newspaper reporter made the estimate but I am surprised, because I thought newspaper men were quite able to make accurate estimates.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take a few minutes to put a few comments on the record in regard to the operation of the United States lines of the Canadian National Railways. The total deficit of all United States lines in 1960, after other income is added but before fixed charges, was $6,856,583, as reported at pages 182 and 183 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the sessional committee. On the same basis there was a deficit of $6,473,732 for the entire C.N.R. system, including the United States lines. Therefore, if the United States operations had been excluded from the C.N.R. statement, the C.N.R. would have shown a profit before fixed1 charges.
The deficit on the U.S. lines after fixed charges was approximately $11 million, as against a total system deficit of $67 million. These are rather fantastic figures when you take them in the context in which I am placing them, because the total investment in United States lines is $186 million against a total system investment of approximately $3,767 million. The United States investment is therefore 5 per cent, but it contributed over 100 per cent of the deficit before fixed charges and 16 per cent of the deficit after fixed charges.
The contention of the railroad is that onward freight received from these United States lines is so valuable and so lucrative to the C.N.R. that it not only wipes out this deficit but provides a profit in the over-all C.N.R. operations. This argument is made on the basis, I assume, that if the C.N.R. did not own these lines it would not have any chance for that freight. Since they have the only tie-in with the United States lines and since they should be somewhat equivalent to the C.P.R. in the efficiency with which they solicit freight and with which they service their customers, I cannot see the validity of that statement.
Furthermore, in the evidence given before the committee one of the chief complaints of the president of the C.N.R. with regard to the difficulty of operating the C.N.R. system in a profitable manner was the fact that the system is a conglomeration of bankrupt railroads and was not built as a single economic entity in the same way as the C.P.R. and that because it is a conglomeration of half a dozen railroads it did not really make economic good sense in many respects.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that these pseudopods stretching down into the United States, these United States lines owned by the C.N.R., are part of the polyglot system and that there has been no effort made by management really to streamline this system in the way of getting rid of these particular lines to which I have referred. It seems to me that

Canadian National Railways it would have been good wisdom to have tried to sell those lines and if they could not be sold then a study should be made of their abandonment and the recapture of whatever can be recaptured from the sale of equipment and real estate because the figures have shown that if we actually gave these lines away the Canadian taxpayer would be in a better position inasmuch as these lines are to all intents and purposes foreign companies that do not contribute anything to the Canadian economy except by way of the onward movement of freight about which the president talks. We are asking and the management have asked the Canadian taxpayer to subsidize to the extent of many millions of dollars a foreign operation. I would say that the management must be prepared to prove what they say. They were asked to give proof and they did not do so. Supposedly there is a report of 150 pages covering a study of this problem, and the key figure in that study must be how much revenue the C.N.R. in Canada derives from the operation of the United States lines. We could not get that figure.
I say that the management should take a good look at the report of the sessional committee and that they should be prepared next time to be able to answer that committee's questions with regard to management. I do not apologize in the least for what somebody criticized as interference with the function of management because I think this loss on United States lines was so glaring and so obvious that it should have been studied a long time ago and the answers should have been clear cut and equally obvious to the committee when the committee members asked these questions.
I do not wish to take any further time except to comment with regard to Trans-Canada Air Lines. In no place have I noticed the fact highlighted that $6.8 million in the surplus account disappeared down the drain because of the rush the air line was in to convert to an all-turbine fleet. We have the first all-turbine operation of any major air line in the world and we have to pay a price to be in that position. That price is the elimination of $6.8 million of a surplus and a deficit of $2 million. This is the real story behind the deficit of T.C.A. Very high depreciation charges have had to be taken. There was the purchase of two Super Constellations for approximately $5 million with a life of seven years but a use under the plan to convert to an all-turbine fleet of only three years. These are the things that are behind the statements and which result in the end in a red figure.

Mr. Speaker, first of all, I wish to be fair to the Minister of Finance. When we were discussing what was involved in the measure at the resolution stage we had a little controversy about the wording of the resolution. I wish to say to my colleagues in the house that I was wrong, that the changes in wording of the resolution were at the end of the resolution and not at the beginning.
The point is that this year we have come to the time when we have to take into account some of the decisions made by parliament a long time ago. I refer to the Canadian National Railways Capital Revision Act of 1952. In sections 4 and 6 there were intimations that after a ten-year period parliament would be asked to review the capital set-up of the C.N.R. I think those features account for the change in the resolution which I criticized the other day.
Hon. members will recognize that this very important measure has been brought before us unduly late in the session. I believe that the resolution only appeared on the order paper on July 6. When we were at the resolution stage the other day I said that I had not been a member of the committee although I had read the relevant portions of the committee's proceedings. I said that the C.N.R. was a key industry in Canada and that, despite what the Minister of Finance might have said in his budget speech, I continued to be alarmed about the C.N.R. because it had not been estimated that in 1961 its revenues would even increase at the rate of 3 per cent. Those of us who are called upon every year to examine this legislation are obliged to look forward to what was forecast by the president of the railway, a deficit very little less than last year, a deficit of $64 million compared with a deficit of $67 million last year.
Last year at this stage of the debate in the House of Commons I said that the Minister of Finance was unrealistic. The last word that he gave us, up to the presentation of this kind of bill, was that the deficit of Canadian National Railways would be between $24 million and $25 million. I said this was wholly unrealistic, having regard to the experience that any one of us sitting here could have observed in the published statements relating to Canadian National Railways and if we were to use as a yardstick the earnings up to that time of Canadian Pacific Railways. I said then, having regard to the earnings of Canadian National, that the deficit would prove to be about three times $24 million. I may have exaggerated a little, but the end result was that the net earnings of Canadian National Railways in 1960 resulted in a deficit of $67 million. I was not too far out a year

ago when I said that, having looked at the first four months of operating revenues and expenses of the railroad.
Yesterday the hon. member for Port Arthur referred to something he called a bombshell, and I think that word is worth repeating. I was not a member of the committee on railways, air lines and shipping, government owned, this year. In that committee, as the hon. member for Port Arthur has stated, the president of Canadian National Railways indicated that there might be another writeoff of the borrowings of the Canadian National to the extent of perhaps $700 million or $900 million. This follows the very important capital revision of this national asset which was made in 1951, and the legislation introduced in 1952. I wonder if the Minister of Finance has advice to give to his colleagues in the House of Commons on this point, as we again have a bill before us to guarantee to this crown corporation a very substantial debt that the corporation might incur in connection with further capital expenditures.
I, of course, have complained, as has the hon. member for Laurier, that this legislation which is an annual item has come to us late in the session, later than I can ever remember as a member of parliament. Because of the lateness we are entitled to expect from the minister, and from the Minister of Transport an up to date report as to the net earnings of this important crown corporation for the first half of 1961. I should like to know whether they are better or worse than the earnings for 1960. When the committee was assembled, we were told the deficit would be $3 million or $4 million less than in 1960. However, I believe that when we are dealing with a bill of this kind we should be told whether or not the earnings for the first six months of this year are better or worse than those of 1960.
I said last year that the Minister of Finance had completely miscalculated or ignored the Canadian National when he told us in parliament that he would have a surplus of $12 million. His calculation at that time was based on a Canadian National deficit of $24 million. Hon. members can see how wrong he was, because the deficit in 1960 proved to be $67 million. I am following in this debate the representative of a neighbouring constituency of mine, the hon. member for Port Arthur, who has taken a great interest in the affairs of Canadian National, just as I have in the past. He is not in his seat, but is apparently hearing what I am saying. I was not a member of the committee on railways, air lines and shipping, government owned, this year, but I was a member of that committee last year for the reasons to which the hon. member for Port Arthur referred,
Canadian National Railways namely the introduction of lay-offs by the Canadian National which were being inaugurated in my constituency and in particular in the town of Sioux Lookout.
I wish to know where the hon. member for Port Arthur stands in connection with some of these matters because they refer to the requirement for capital murder under the bill before us. When I was a member of the committee last year I asked the committee to hear, not the Sioux Lookout representatives of labour unions and organizations, but regional representations from western, eastern and other areas. This can be confirmed by looking at pages 19, 20 and 22 of the report of the hearings of the committee last year. As I have said, I was not a member of the committee this year, but apparently the hon. member for Port Arthur wished to hear union representations in connection with turnaround rights and pension rights. He wanted these people to be heard by our House of Commons committee. Last year, as is indicated by reference to page 19 of the committee report, he voted against the motion that I made asking that unions be heard with this matter in mind.
A great many suggestions have been made with regard to improving the efficiency of the Canadian National Railways. There was a suggestion from the government that we should have another write-off of capital obligations. According to the evidence of the president of the C.N.R. before the committee, this might involve $700 million or $900 million. At a rough guess, with tight money this might involve an annual income responsibility of $40 million. Therefore when the committee was asked to consider a deficit of $64 million for 1961, in the future they might be able to write off $40 million of debt because the capital obligation had been transferred from the crown corporation to the Minister of Finance. I ask the Minister of Finance to speak about this. There was a large write-off in 1951. Is there in contemplation another write-off of this volume?
I have here a sessional paper which was produced in the House of Commons when the present Minister of Finance sat on this side of the house. It was moved by Senator Pouliot, the then member for Temiscouata. There are many questions on this sessional paper but I propose to read only one or two. Question No. 1 reads as follows:
Did the cancellation of capital stocks and certain indebtedness of the Canadian National railway system to His Majesty, in virtue of chapter 22 of 1 George VI (1937), amount to more than $1,200,000,000, and what was the exact amount of that cancellation?
The answer provided at that time was that indeed it did; it amounted to a reduction of

Canadian National Railways $900 million. The hon. member for Port Arthur has referred to a possible further reduction of obligation and of debt to the extent of somewhere between $700 million and $900 million. If one refers to the minister's remarks of July 6 one finds that there is apparently crossing his mind the idea of doing this all over again. We were persuaded that if we introduced new capital into the C.N.R., which over a period of perhaps ten years amounted to an increase in capital of approximately $1 billion, it would result in efficiency, earning power, and so on of the railways that would produce not a deficit but a surplus.
What is the answer to this question? Does the Minister of Finance agree with the hon. member for Port Arthur that perhaps, as was suggested by the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett years ago, we should have amalgamation of these two railways? Certainly it was clearly the view of the hon. member for Port Arthur when he said on February 27, 1961, as reported at page 2479 of Hansard:
*-the whole railway operation in Canada should be consolidated under a government corporation.
What is that going to do with respect to employment? Are we going to eliminate competition between railways in this country? Is that what the hon. member for Port Arthur had in mind when he said that what we want is consolidation of the two railways of this country under a government corporation?
I say that is tantamount to accepting what was turned down by the electorate in 1935 when the late Right Hon. R. B. Bennett proposed the same thing and was voted out. When we read the minister's remarks in introducing the resolution we have what I call an apology, a procrastination, a deferment that is typical of this administration. The minister points out that under the decisions of parliament in 1951 or 1952 we decided there would be deferment of certain debt obligations of the Canadian National Railways, but parliament said that they would start to bear interest after ten years. Those decisions like the proverbial chickens have come home to roost this year.
What the minister is proposing in this bill is that he should have another year to procrastinate and not make a decision. I say that must be considered before we approve the bill before us. This means another year of procrastination. I refer to section 3 of the Canadian National Railways Refunding Act of 1955. This refers to the matter the minister mentioned in his resolution speech with respect to the $200 million opportunity of the railway for freedom in this field.
In addition I refer to the $100 million item to which the minister referred in his speech

on July 6. There again is an extension for one year of freedom from any obligation on the part of the Canadian National Railways to pay interest on the $100 million item. This is typical of this government. They are just procrastinating and deferring, until after an election, decisions that I suggest have to be made now.
I ask the minister, this government and all supporters of this government whether or not they have looked or are continuing to look at the balance sheets of these two competing national railways, C.P.R. and C.N.R. I pointed out last year that the capital expenditure asked by the competitor to our national railroad was $83 million, including $25 million for their air arm, which would bring down that amount considerably. I asked how the cabinet, which must approve these things, compared that with the requirement for which we were asked, which I think on a comparable basis, including T.C.A., was $197 million. Are we getting results from decisions of this kind which have to be approved by cabinet? I know that this crown company has certain opportunities. I also know the minister has said in this house that any crown company must be treated in the same way as any other corporation. On that basis, is this capital being generated and provided under intelligent and careful supervision by the cabinet of this country? This information would be interesting to all members of this House of Commons and of particular interest to those who support this government.
We hear that within a year there may be a possibility that the obligation to subscribe for preferred stock of the Canadian National Railways based on the act of 1951 and based on the company's annual earnings may be discontinued. I hope the minister will make it clear what kind of careful study has been made with respect to this. The statutes are clear. It is now ten years since the statute was enacted in parliament, and two or three at least of these chickens have come home to roost. The minister is taking an attitude which, I say, is typical of this government. He and his colleagues are deferring a decision. They have nothing to tell us, except that in the last three or four clauses of this bill they ask for another year in which to make up their minds.

No, I am not referring to any hon. member in particular. I think my remarks apply equally to all, and if you will bear with me for a few minutes I will try to explain why I say that. We all acknowledge

that it is the duty of every member to represent his constituents in this house and to put forward their grievances and their requests. We should do that, I think, in a reasonable manner and we do not portray a reasonable picture to the public when we place on Hansard a picture of a small part of the situation without projecting that against the background of the whole picture. We all receive letters from our constituents Which set forth certain grievances as they appear to our constituents. Very often these letters present only part of the evidence. If we are going to present a picture to the public, I think it is only fair to the C.N.R. and to the public as well to place alongside of that the picture as it appears to the management.
We all know that Canadian National Railways face very severe problems, and these problems are rooted in history. In the eastern part of Canada, the maritime provinces, these problems go right back to confederation because one of the terms under which the maritime provinces agreed to confederate with Upper Canada was that a railway should be built. It was envisaged that that railway would link up central Canada with the eastern seaboard to transport the products of central Canada to the east coast. In this way the eastern seaports would be built up, and this would be beneficial to all. However, that did not happen. It was ten years before the railway was built, although that was one of the terms of confederation.
When the railway was built, it was not built in accordance with economic requirements, but mainly for military purposes. The railway did not serve the economic needs of the area. Various other lines came into existence which could not possibly be operated economically and so, in time, they went bankrupt. Pressure was put on the central government to take them over. Finally, these bankrupt lines, with their overhead and their debts, became part of the financial structure of the Canadian National Railways. Before things could be straightened out, wars intervened. During the last war when steel was scarce and could not be spared to build up the railway lines, these lines became rapidly exhausted. After the war, the Canadian National Railways was faced with broken down lines and with all the problems arising out of the accumulation of these bankrupt lines. In addition, the railway was faced with increasing demands from employees for better wages, better working conditions and the demands that we, ourselves, make in this house from time to time.
It is too much to expect that any human being could overcome all these difficulties, modernize all the broken down equipment,

meet the wage demands, and still operate without a deficit. I think the fact that this was done in some years is in itself a testimony to the efficiency of the C.N.R. management. I say that because when we consider that the C.N.R. comprises nearly 35,000 miles of track, 104,000 employees and an expenditure of over $700 million per year, the very vastness of that organization is almost beyond the average person's comprehension.
The Canadian National Railways is a vital part of our communications system. It is a part of our lifeline. In my own province it is our lifeline. Transportation problems are difficult in every country, but in a country like Canada, with such vast areas to be served and with such a small population distributed in a very thin line along the southern border, those problems are much more difficult than we perhaps find in any other country of the world with the exception of China.
We must endeavour to find the best solution we can to these problems. The solution found must be fair to other segments of the transportation industry. I am thinking particularly of the truck lines. Canadian National Railways has been more or less forced into the trucking industry, in the public interest, to keep its deficits as small as possible and to meet the competition of the trucking industry. I do not think anyone wants the C.N.R. to get into the trucking industry and compete unfairly with the private segments of that industry. That was a major concern of some members of the committee.
In this connection I wish to say that our leader has received a number of telegrams from the trucking industry on this subject. We thoroughly agree that there should be no cut rates for the sake of unfair competition which might endanger the private sector of the trucking industry. Mr. Gordon himself gave an assurance in this regard, as recorded at page 271 of the report of the proceedings of the committee. The hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) said:
I want to bring to your attention that I have had some concern and have had a number of representations from employees in the trucking industry who have expressed the feeling that in some circumstances some of the firms, who knew they would be acquired by the railway, were quoting low rates.

I think I can give you this positive assurance that it is no part of our policy to engage in unfair competition, or unfair competitive practices in the trucking industry. It is my own belief that the entry of the railways, and particularly the Canadian National Railways into the trucking industry, will have a most salutary effect in regard to the ethics of the business. I am talking about maintenance of rates, overloading, the observance of franchise requirements, and so on. I can certify that the Canadian National does not in any way break the law and will not. We have already found some practices which we could not countenance and we have changed them. I would repeat
Canadian National Railways what I have said, that our entry into the business will have a very beneficial effect on the whole standard of the industry.
Some hon. members may hold a different opinion, but I think we have here a clear statement of policy on behalf of the management of the C.N.R. It is not only a statement of policy but an assurance that there will be no unfair competition in the trucking industry. If evidence accumulates to the contrary, then of course there will be another opportunity at the next committee hearing to pursue further questioning on that point.
The second question which concerned the committee a good deal was the morale of the employees of the C.N.R. I believe everyone will agree that morale is important in every industry, but in no industry is it perhaps more important than in the Canadian National Railways. The morale of any industry is certainly the duty of the management, but it is no less the duty of the employees. Particularly it is the duty and responsibility of the leadership of the employees and employee organizations. It is no less our duty in this house to contribute to that morale. We do not contribute and in fact I think we tend to undermine morale in the Canadian National Railways when we make attacks based on faulty or incomplete evidence and when we speak in an intemperate manner. We are not contributing to the morale of the Canadian National Railways by the way in which we are now treating the present president and the board of directors.
As was pointed out this morning by the hon. member for Laurier, we are being asked to vote large sums of money without knowing what is going to happen to the present president; without knowing who will be in charge of the spending of this money. We do not know who will be on the board of directors, directing the management and the affairs of the railway. I do not think any conscientious person can say that is contributing to the morale of the employees of Canadian National Railways.
There is also another aspect of this matter. It is an affront to parliament itself. We have heard much in recent days about the supremacy of parliament, but parliament is not merely the executive; it is not merely the Prime Minister. Parliament is all of us in this house and the other place. Hon. members on the other side of the house have just as much responsibility as we in the opposition to see that the rights of parliament and the supremacy of parliament are preserved. Therefore if we really believe in the supremacy of parliament, certainly the information as to who is going to be the president of the railway and who are going

Canadian National Railways to fill the extra seats on the board of directors should be made known to parliament before this bill is passed.
I think the morale of the Canadian National Railways could make a great contribution to the morale of the country as a whole, because the C.N.R. is in a very special position in that it extends right across the country from east to west; it serves all sections and all districts of our country, and if we had in the C.N.R. a high level of morale, that would be an example for other industries to follow and it would also, I think, inspire and uplift the morale of the other parts of Canada.

We learned from Mr. Gordon in the committee that very often the employees themselves neglect to act in their own interest, particularly with respect to pension contributions. It was only a few years ago, after trying all voluntary methods without success, that Mr. Gordon and the management found it necessary to make pension contributions compulsory. As long as contributions were not compulsory a large percentage of the employees neglected to make 
their contributions, though it was clearly in their own interest that they should do so.
I have a great deal of sympathy for the former employees of the C.N.R. and, indeed, for all civil servants who retired at a time when pensions were small. We are now faced with a problem in this respect and I believe parliament will have to deal with it, particularly in connection with those who retired on $25 a month. Some 40 years ago, $25 a month might have been a significant sum, but today it is not even pin money and it is clearly not possible for people to exist on such a pittance; it must certainly be supplemented from charity. I think we have an obligation in this direction, but in many cases these situations arise out of the failure of the employees themselves to act in their own interest.
I said that the Canadian National Railways was of particular importance to my own province because it is the only railway we have. Transportation is the greatest problem we face with respect to the industrial development of our province. We have many small, secondary industries, which are capable of competing in the mainland market as far as their operating costs and efficiency are concerned, but when the freight rates are added the picture is changed and it is made impossible for them to compete. We know that this problem of freight rates is under study and we hope that this study will produce a solution which will replace the present system of horizontal increases in freight rates. That practice, which has been carried on, now, for many years, has practically destroyed the original benefits of the Maritime Freight Rates Act. We are also in need of increased services in my province although, as the manager of the C.N.R. pointed out to us, considerable debt is incurred on the services we already have. Mr. Speaker, we are being asked by the government to authorize the provision of moneys to meet certain capital expenditures of the Canadian National Railways system for the period from the 1st day of January 1961 to the 30th day 90205-6-490
Canadian National Railways of June 1962. As this is a crown corporation, we must of course give full consideration to the matter.
In considering the problem, we should take into account the plans of the C.N.R., as well as the situation of the trucking industry in the province of Quebec and in the whole of Canada.
In that connection, Mr. Speaker, I received a telegram on July 6-I think a copy was sent to all hon. members-signed by Mr. Romeo Blouin, secretary general of the Quebec trucking association incorporated. The telegram reads as follows:
Are informed C.N.R. is asking Quebec provincial transport board to acquire trucking companies stop We protest against railway interference in field of private enterprise stop On behalf of our members urgently request your intervention in favour of private enterprise against state monopoly.
Mr. Speaker, after receiving this telegram, a member on the government side asked a question on the subject to the Minister of Transport, and here is the minister's reply, as recorded on page 7680 of Hansard for July 7 1961:
Mr. Speaker, that is a decision for the authorities of the C.N.R. However, I should like to assure my hon. friend that I will pass on to the C.N.R. officials the representations he has made in that connection.
Mr. Speaker, following that reply from the minister, I asked the following question:
Mr. Speaker, could the minister take that opportunity to impress upon the C.N.R. that it should not enter a field which belongs to private enterprise, especially the trucking industry?
And the Minister of Transport answered:
The final decision as to whether or not the C.N.R. will be allowed to purchase or operate a trucking business in the province of Quebec, rests with the Quebec transport board.
So the Minister of Transport promised the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Bel-zile) that he would make appropriate representations to the Canadian National authorities, and I very much hope that my brief remarks this afternoon in connection with this matter will prompt him further to communicate with the Canadian National authorities to make them understand the need of that industry, of which all hon. members are aware.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian National Railways Company has already started to acquire some trucking companies in the country. The trucking industry is apprehensive of its fate at the thought that the C.N.R. will become, if it is not already, a competitor in that field.

Canadian National Railways
That association worries the more about the present situation as it is made up of representatives of the whole trucking industry in this country.
The Canadian trucking association incorporated last June presented a brief to the Prime Minister and to the members of the cabinet. In the introduction to this brief can be found the names of the various member organizations throughout the country. As the brief says:
The provincial trucking associations comprise over 6,000 trucking companies, including interprovincial and extra-provincial trucking firms.
Those companies provide every imaginable service with regard to renting local and long distance transportation for goods.
The total volume of commodities moved from city to city by renting transportation companies, according to the brief, and as indicated by the dominion bureau of statistics, amounted to 140,504,000 tons in 1958. Those figures mentioned in the brief were supplied by the dominion bureau of statistics.
I need not add, Mr. Speaker, that the industry receives no assistance whatsoever either from the provinces or from the central government. A subsidy is granted to the crown corporation which operates a railway service and now wants to buy out trucking companies. The government is thus being prejudicial to the trucking industry. Let nobody in the government tell us that they are promoting private industry. The Prime Minister may voice high sounding statements to the effect that the next election platform will be the protection of private enterprise against socialism, but he is only misleading the people.
Unfortunately, I do not have before me that newspaper item containing the statement I just quoted. But he publicly stated that the next election would have as its theme: "private enterprise versus socialism."
If the Prime Minister is ready to defend private enterprise, the members of his cabinet, and more particularly the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) should not wait until election time to set an example.
I remember a recent letter from a transport company in Winnipeg, complaining that another carrier, the east-west company, transported goods at prices which might mean bankruptcy for other carriers. We should not only help these firms not to founder, but we should protect them against those who, for some reason or other, are willing to work


under conditions which others could not afford. Moreover, the government has the responsibility to protect private companies against crown companies or even against the Canadian National Railways, who want to interfere in the trucking industry.
I should like to draw hon. members' attention to the following view which is to be found on page 3 of the brief:
-it has already been suggested that the trucking industry did not pay its fair share of road costs, and consequently, that it is subsidized by the Canadian taxpayer. The trucking industry does not travel free of charge on Canada's highways. And the industry is not subsidized, whether directly or indirectly. In registration and licensing fees and gasoline taxes, the commercial road carrier contributes much more, proportionately, to the revenues of government treasuries than the private car owner. And contributions will continue on such a scale, as all informed Canadians know.
The members of this association, Mr. Chairman, do not object to the C.N.R. authorities doing business in transportation. They accept competition, but want fair competition. On the other hand, they claim-and I support this contention-that crown corporations should not try to cut the throats of those who pay taxes in order to pay for the deficits of crown corporations.
Mr. Chairman, mention is also made in the same brief of a statement of principles made by the province of Quebec. It appears on page 6 of the brief, and also in the official record of proceedings of the royal commission on transportation, volume 124, page 20664. I quote:
We believe that the problem facing the people of Canada and the people of Quebec is not a matter of favouring one method of transportation at the expense of another. Rather than that, we should ask ourselves what is the most efficient means of providing useful transportation services, on a long range national basis, and what is the best way of providing the services at the lowest possible cost to the consumer without adding to the load of the Canadian taxpayer. We therefore believe that each of the five main types of transportation are the instruments of national policy, and that economic and national interests should be the guiding criteria.
I shall not delve further into the subject, hoping that the Minister of Transport, who promised this week to bring the situation to the attention of the C.N.R. management, will take the necessary action and perhaps will be able to persuade the C.N.R. to change its policy in this field.
Now just a few words on another subject. Under the bill now before us, we are asked to vote something close to $179 million,

including $19,700,000 for the financial needs of Trans-Canada Air Lines.
This morning, I asked a question of the minister to find out how things stood with regard to the work stoppage at T.C.A., which is to take effect on July 21.
I hope, as I mentioned this morning, that the government will do its utmost to prevent this strike, which would deprive thousands of citizens of this transportation service for an indefinite length of time.
I hope the government is giving serious consideration to this matter and will be much quicker in providing a solution than it has been in fulfilling its promise to tackle the unemployment situation which is now plaguing the country.

I greatly appreciate the language used by the universally respected member for Greenwood in his remarks which can be found in Hansard of May 13, 1961. He said, as some other hon. members did, it is unfortunate that our committee members are so sensitive about a president on 90205-6-490J
Canadian National Railways occasion speaking back to the members of this house. Whoever we have in this important office-and the appointment should not be delayed-should be a man and not a mouse. If that kind of man is appointed I am sure that after the next election the new administration will be very happy to work with him, just as former Liberal administrations were able to work so co-operatively with outstanding men such as Clifford Clark and Graham Towers who were appointed by a Conservative government. We want a man of courage and independent judgment. This is the type of person we want right throughout our public service and heading all our crown corporations.
I should like to quote a few words that Adlai Stevenson used on television a few months ago. He said:
More important than winning the election is governing the nation. This is the final test of a political party, the acid final test. When the tumult and the shouting die there remains the stark reality of responsibility.
I feel, sir, that governing a country, with problems as complex as those of Canada, calls for skills and ability on the part of key public servants probably exceeding those that are necessary even to preside over ministries.
May 1 turn to a matter of historic interest, namely the Brockville railway station. This is a subject that has commanded the attention of this parliament in years past. George T. Fulford and my predecessor, Hayden Stanton, both expressed themselves in strong terms about our station. While it is of considerable interest to local historians we feel that this building erected I think in the month of June, 1856, as the terminal of the Grand Trunk Railway, has perhaps outlived its functional usefulness. Now we would like to present it to Upper Canada Village.
I was able to find in the library of parliament a book entitled "A Souvenir of Brockville". Judging by the costumes, the bicycles, the hoop skirts and so on depicted in the illustrations I think it was probably produced about the time of Queen Victoria's jubilee. I see parasols in sailboats, paddlewheels and things of that kind. The only thing in those photographs of early Brockville that really reminds one of the Brockville of today are the islands and, of course, the post office which the Minister of Public Works has so recently promised to replace very shortly and our station.
I spoke to a telegrapher who went to Brockville in 1901. He tells me that in those days the station looked exactly as it does today. I think that is not quite correct because, fortuitously, between July 26 and August 3, 1910 there was a Grand Trunk strike during which some damage was done

Canadian National Railways to the station. I say fortuitously because after the windows and the doors were repaired our station was smartened up just a bit. Since that time, except for the addition of flush toilets, there has been no change for the better.
Now we see certain changes that are disturbing. We find that the yard office, which is being discontinued, now occupies a comer of the old station. In place of two waiting rooms we now have one. The express depot at the station is being shifted to a freight shed. The car repair division of the Manitoba yards and the brake inspection department are being cut down and the operation of shops curtailed.
We do recognize that certain things must give way to progress. It may be that there have to be fundamental changes affecting our railroad families, but there was a time when in Brockville there were 700 to 800 railroaders. These were great people. They are the people who laid the foundation of my Thousand islands city, and their descendants have contributed very largely to the progress of this country. We now have fast diesel freights going right through Brockville, and whatever happens in the future earnest regard must be given to what will happen to the railroaders of Brockville who are involved.
In 1854 Brockville was the end of the line for anyone travelling to western Canada from Montreal. People then took a boat and travelled by water up the river past Kingston to Belleville. But now the situation is different. Brockville is almost midway between the two great metropolitan areas of Montreal and Toronto. I put it to the house earnestly that Brockville is in the most exciting area for new industrial development in Canada. We have the facilities in eastern Ontario for far reaching industrial expansion. If any part of Canada is bound to go forward in the next decade, it surely is this part, I urge the administration to please give us a new station and very soon.
