speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier, the matter at hand involves public funds exceeding $200 million to enable the C.N.R. to make capital expenditures during the calendar year of 1960 in the amount of $178 million and at the same time to authorize expenditures of $76 million for 1962, in addition to other expenses of $44 million.
Those amounts include expenditures with regard to road property and, if I am not mistaken, this means the maintenance of many miles of railway tracks owned by railway companies, including the C.N.R., as well as the bridges scattered over thousands of miles of railways belonging to that company.
Well, I have a point I wish to bring to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and, in this matter, he would want to relay our suggestions and recommendations to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) who is more directly responsible for consulting with C.N.R. authorities. It is a most important matter which I think has not been raised in the house. It has to do with passenger safety.
I had the oportunity, in 1958, to remind the house that in my district alone, that is the Levis district, there had been 80 section gangs and that, in the autumn of 1957, their number was reduced from 80 to 50. As an engineer and one with some experience in the construction of bridges, I am well aware of the dangers of leaving bridges in such a condition that they constitute a threat for the travelling public. In fact, each year there are millions of persons travelling on our trains, trusting that railway authorities do their best to keep bridges and railways in good repair.
Well, when you find that a division comprising 80 sections or 80 gangs looking after

the tracks, has been reduced, you wonder whether passenger safety is being adequately provided for today. It is a known fact and I know it in my capacity as an engineer that, particularly in the spring at flood time, the water in a river will often erode the abutment piers of a bridge. That is why I find it deplorable that the number of these maintenance gangs has been reduced.
You know by experience, Mr. Speaker, what care is taken by air lines and how everything is checked before the plane leaves.
I wonder why the same precautions are not taken in the case of railways on which, as I say, millions of passengers are travelling each year. I draw once again the attention of the minister to this point for I believe it is an important one. It may be said that there has been no serious accident so far. That may be so. But, on the other hand, who knows what the future holds? That is why I ask the minister to get in touch with the management of the C.N.R. and to make them understand that if they must cut down some expenses they should not however endanger the security of the travelling public.
I should like to draw the attention of the house to another aspect of the question. It concerns a recommendation in the report of the sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping-unfortunately, I do not have the French copy with me-to the effect that continuous efforts be made in order to increase the corporate feeling and the confidence among employees. I believe that this is an important aspect of the question. I do not intend to belabour the point for it seems to me that the relations between management and labour have their importance in a company which numbers nearly 100,000 employees.
I am glad to see that the committee has particularly drawn the attention of the railway authorities on this subject, and I will not deal with it any longer. I have had the opportunity in the past to prove that the morale of the employees is low at the present time, for the simple reason that when statistics tell them that each year 4,000 or 5,000 railway employees with 15, 20 or 25 years of service are fired, they have reason to fear, for they live in uncertainty, not knowing what tomorrow holds for them.
Well, as I said, I am glad that the committee has drawn that problem to the attention of the railways, and I hope that the
Canadian National Railways management will not only read the report, but that they will carry out its recommendations.
I believe that all companies today have their personnel division. Well, I think steps will have to be taken in order to give railway employees the feeling they are doing a worthwhile job and that they are in no danger of losing their jobs at a moment's notice. Because we know that there are not many railways here in Canada, and when a railroader loses his job, it is quite difficult for him to rehabilitate himself in another company.
There is another point with which I should like to deal, sir, that of the administrative system reorganization. I mentioned that in January and I mention it again today because, apparently, nothing has been done about it.
In the past, we had three regions: the Atlantic region, the Central region and the Pacific region. Today, we have five: Atlantic, St. Lawrence, Great Lakes, prairies and mountain.
In January I pointed out-I cannot repeat all I said then-that due to management reorganization, a section in the province of Quebec was attached to the Atlantic region.
I make that remark because the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Creaghan) seemed to think at that time that I was opposed to the headquarters for that region being in Moncton.
Such thoughts were far from my mind because in my opinion the place I just mentioned is truly the logical center of operations for that region.
However, there is a fact I oppose, and I am not the only one who takes that position.
Mr. Speaker, you had an opportunity yourself to see in the newspapers of our district representations made by the municipal councils and various public bodies concerned giving the reasons for their action. Those reasons had nothing to do with matters of language nor were they inspired by fanaticism.
The matter was only of an administrative nature which could bring more benefits to the district extending from Riviere du Loup through the Matapedia valley, to Campbell-ton and Gaspe. I hope that even though the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) is not here, my remarks will reach the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer).

I hope that this matter will again be taken up with the railway authorities so that this section I mentioned earlier may become a part of the St. Lawrence rather than of the Atlantic region.
Those Mr. Speaker, were the few remarks I wanted to make. I tried to make them as short as possible.
And as they usually say on the government side, I hope those matters will be duly and seriously considered by the government.

speechtext:
This afternoon we are considering in this bill the requirements of Canadian National Railways, a great national enterprise. It is an enterprise, however, which has operated under great difficulties for a number of years. It is a federation of many companies put into business for various reasons at various times, and has assumed liabilities which put it in a uniquely difficult position to compete, not only with the other major railway system in this country but also with other forms of transportation. Canadian National has a capital structure which is complicated and, in the opinion of many people, onerous.
To those, Mr. Speaker, who are interested in state planning, the growth and development of the railway systems of this country makes an interesting story. The technical changes which we have seen throughout the years were impossible to foresee. Not only do we have in many places an excess of rail capacity, but new modes of transportation have arisen to provide competition which could not possibly have been anticipated during the period when the railway systems were inaugurated. Who could have foreseen, at the turn of the century, what the future would hold? Who could foresee what the advent of the airplane would do to travel concepts?
In 1959, Mr. Speaker, we celebrated the 50th anniversary of powered flight in Canada. From a time when an airplane was able to fly only a few yards across the ice, we have now come to the point in the evolution of this miraculous machine where airplanes can travel thousands of miles at very high speeds. May I say in passing that I regret the recent death of the pilot of the first aircraft, Air Commodore McCurdy.
Air transportation has undergone a gradually explosive evolution. I remember as a boy on the farm those beautiful silver winged aircraft, the DC-3's, as they passed over en route from Buffalo to Detroit. I recall the glamour that they had and the spirit of adventure which seemed to lay behind them. I watched with great interest the evolution


which has taken place in the aircraft industry since that time. The DC-3 was the first great workhorse of the air lines, the aircraft which really put modern air line companies into business. It has just recently been retired from service on our major air lines in Canada but is still in service elsewhere throughout the world. Each successive aircraft has been more comfortable and faster. We have had in this country a succession of aircraft designs to the point where Trans-Canada Air Lines now boasts the position of being the first all-jet air line.
We have all heard the stories from the second world war of those hair-raising flights across the Atlantic ocean in bucket seats, with oxygen masks. We have heard some of the interesting and exciting tales of dangerous and unforgettable flights not only into danger in the service of this country in the pursuit of winning the war. Since then aircraft have been designed and put into service which make those aircraft seem like antiques of another age. Turbo jet and pure jet engines have made a tremendous contribution to the development of not only safe but comfortable air travel. Trans-Canada Air Lines main fleet of turbo jet aircraft is capable of flying at speeds in the range of 285 to 350 miles per hour. This reduces the air travel time between points in Canada very substantially indeed.
Then of course with the advent of the pure jet engine more recently-the DC-8's with speeds of approximately 550 miles per hour- the travelling time has been almost cut in half from that of the turbo prop aircraft. Today we have very comfortable air travel at very high altitudes. This, again, is a departure from previous days and has only been made possible with the pure jet engine. When flying at altitudes of approximately 35,000 feet one usually flies above the weather on a smooth course and with all the luxury and comfort of home or the club.
Of course, the end is not yet in sight. Supersonic aircraft are on the drawing boards which will triple the speed of existing jet air-liners. Aircraft with speeds of 1,500 miles per hour are now in military service and it is only a matter of a few short years until aircraft of comparable speeds will be introduced into commercial air line service. When that becomes a reality it will be possible to fly from Ottawa to Europe, for example, in two hours, or from Ottawa to Vancouver in a comparable time. We will have a two-hour flight from coast to coast or from one side of the ocean to the other side of the ocean. It is almost unbelievable, and yet this has all taken place within a period of a few decades.
As the speed of aircraft increases the ground time due to inadequate planning and traffic

congestion is becoming an increasing proportion of the total travel time. But notwithstanding this confusion on the ground it is still possible to travel very great distances in relatively very short periods of time. All this has a direct bearing on rail transport. People who in previous times travelled by train now prefer to travel by air. Just as the automobile and the autobus have provided1 great competition for trains on short runs, so the airplane has largely supplanted long range train travel. As wages and salaries rise time becomes more valuable, and time saved' by air travel on long hauls more than compensates for any small difference in the fares.
In addition to air travel the trains are now subject to another form of competition. With the opening of large sections of the trans-Canada highway the casual traveller who is not in a great hurry can enjoy the flexibility of scenic highway travel in the luxury of his own auto. This great Canadian achievement inaugurated, as most great Canadian achievements have been, under the previous Liberal administration is adding tremendously to the flexibility of Canadian transportation. We hope it will not be too long before it will be possible to drive from coast to coast on the trans-Canada highway.

speechtext:
We started it and I would not be surprised, bearing in mind the speed with which the present government is progressing, if we are able to open it also. With the completion of large sections of this highway it is possible for truck transport to compete more favourably with other forms of transportation. The net result of these various forms of competition is a falling off of passenger traffic for our railroads and the occurrence of heavy losses. Indeed, we have been told that the day of the trans-continental passenger train may be near an end. This raises a feeling of nostalgia for anyone who has ever travelled across the country by train. It also raises the very real question as to whether or not in the national interest it is desirable to maintain at least a minimum rail service on the main routes.
There are many questions involved. For example there is the question of weather. As any air traveller knows, there are sometimes periods of days, sometimes stretching into a week or more, when the weather at a terminal point is not satisfactory for air travel and when landing conditions are such that air travel is not allowed because of safety requirements. During these periods it is often
Canadian National Railways necessary for travellers to avail themselves of train services regardless of their usual travelling habits.
There is also the question of national safety and survival. What would we do in the case of nuclear attack, for example? Would the railroads be required to move personnel and supplies? Just what precautions should be taken in the national interest in order to keep a minimum service available in case it is required? This question should be investigated and a decision made with all the factors in mind. If a subsidy is necessary to maintain a service, the cost will have to be equated with the benefit. At least at the outset the question of whether or not a minimum service should be maintained on the major national routes should be determined. If it is considered in the public interest that such a service should be maintained, then the financial aspect should be taken into consideration. If it requires subsidies, this is something that would have to be done as a result of the national policy.
In their freight services, too, the railroads are subject to much competition. It was not long ago that many of us had the opportunity of travelling to Montreal to witness the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway. It was a grand occasion, with Her Majesty the Queen and the President of the United States in attendance. Visiting dignitaries from both sides of the border joined hands in a great international transportation project. It was a day which will long be remembered in the history of this country. But it was not just the day which will be remembered. It was the work which went into that great project, the culmination of a dream of decades-the culmination of an engineering project which taxed the imagination of the whole world. Now the St. Lawrence seaway ranks as one of the great engineering marvels of the world and contributes to a great internal waterway as part of the Canadian transport system.
In addition, there has been phenomenal growth in the trucking industry. This has proved to be a very flexible form of cargo handling. It has many advantages. A truck can be loaded and unloaded at the points of origin and destination without the cargo having to be transshipped. On many types of haul it is cheaper as well as more flexible to use this type of transportation. With the opening of large sections of the trans-Canada highway, the growth of the trucking industry will undoubtedly increase, and as it does so competition between the trucking industry and the railroad will become keener.

Canadian National Railways
I have received a number of complaints with respect to subsidies granted by parliament to the railroads. But it should be remembered that the railroads are not the only form of public transport to have been subsidized by the Canadian taxpayer. Almost since the early days of this country it has been necessary for the public to subsidize one form of transportation after another beginning, first of all, with the canals. The canals of this country were built at great expense. For example, until the St. Lawrence seaway was opened no tolls were charged on the Welland canal even though its construction had involved a considerable initial capital outlay. Even since the opening of the seaway the recovery from tolls on the canal has been designed to recoup only the additional cost of making that canal suitable for shipping of deeper draught which is now able to use the canal. By and large, throughout the history of this country, tolls have not been collected on our canal system. In addition, dockage charges have in no respect been sufficient to recover for the federal treasury the large capital outlays which were required to build them in the first instance. The fact is that the whole of our canal and shipping facilities, which have required a tremendous capital outlay, were in the first instance provided as a public service to contribute to the growth and development of our transportation system to serve all the Canadian people.
The second major development was the railroads. Here again, millions of dollars have been involved in subsidies from the time when the railroads were first built. It was a deliberate decision based on national policy that the Canadian people should make capital and land available in order to permit and encourage the development of railroads in order that there might be a Canadian nation. This remains national policy. It is part of the price of Canadian nationhood.
Now I turn to the trucking industry. Here again, highways from coast to coast have been built at public expense. There are few, if any, toll collections on Canadian roads. There are some, as you know, Mr. Speaker, in the United States. They have a number of toll "thruways". It has been suggested that it might be a good idea if we were to follow their example and build some toll roads. But the Canadian temperament thus far has been of contrary mind. Thus far it has provided roads as a public service and made them available to all the citizens of this country as well as to visitors who come here from other countries. But in so doing, the Canadian taxpayers, through their various levels of government, national, provincial and municipal, have been obliged to pay hundreds of millions of dollars in order that


an acceptable network of roads and highways through our various provinces, and now from coast to coast, might be built. It is true we do have a few bridges, including international bridges, on which tolls are collected, but these are an exception rather than the standard practice. Hundreds of millions of dollars in subsidies are involved in the roads which are a foundation of the trucking part of our transportation industry.
Finally, I turn to air travel. Again, very heavy public subsidies have been required. These subsidies, if they have not already done so, will soon run into hundreds of millions of dollars. One need only examine the cost of new terminal facilities at our great travel centres, such as Montreal, Toronto and the other great cities across the country to realize this and to realize also the cost of building and extending runways to meet the needs of modern jet transport.
I remember Mr. Justice Abbott when he was minister of finance talking of the very heavy public participation in the building up of an air transportation system in Canada. Again, this was a matter of national policy. It has always been a matter of pride that our national air line, Trans-Canada Air Lines, has been able to pay its way, having many surpluses during the course of its operation. This has been a matter of pride to the shareholders, the Canadian nation, but it must be realized that in order that this might be done it has been necessary, first of all, to give Trans-Canada Air Lines the privilege of a monopoly arrangement in serving the major traffic areas of this country. At the same time, no effort has been made to collect tolls which would be sufficient to pay for the terminal facilities and runways at our Canadian airports. These have been paid from the public purse.
It is not conclusive for any one form of transportation in Canada to complain about the subsidy of any other. In order to be able to consider these complaints with some objectivity it would be necessary to have some basis for comparison. To the best of my knowledge transportation subsidies have usually been treated on an ad hoc basis. Perhaps this has been inevitable as our country grew and developed from infancy. However, I feel now the time has come when we should seek some over-all comparative standard.
I am not suggesting it is desirable or nec-cessary to try to equate the subsidy in each. I do not know; it may be desirable to try to do so, then again it might not be desirable. At least it would be helpful to have some sort of standard at which to look. I would, therefore, recommend that a royal commission be appointed to examine into

the history and development of the major forms of transportation in Canada, and in particular to determine in so far as possible the extent of public subsidy involved in each existing major form of transportation.
I realize that such a study would not be easy. The difference in purchasing power of currency from time to time, for example, would have to be equated, but I am convinced that would be a worthwhile exercise and that the result would act as a guide to parliament and to the Canadian people when considering public transportation policy. It might also provide some interesting information to those persons engaged in the transportation field who believe that each of the competing systems is subsidized unfairly to the detriment of their own particular position.
In recommending the appointment of a royal commission I would say that I should not expect it would make a report before the next general election, and that after the election it would report to a new government not only capable of benefiting from the information but capable of taking action if action seemed to be necessary following the report.
This bill before us today also involves an ad hoc measure. It commits the government of Canada to very sizeable obligations and the question arises as to where the money will come from. It is not sufficient to meet the demands of private development when added to that figure is the public capital expenditure, the public current deficit and the other cash requirements such as those I have just mentioned, including those set out in the bill now before us.

Very shortly, Mr. Speaker, on the 1st of September the same thing will occur in the riding of Lincoln where the city of St. Catharines has received notice from the C.N.R. of the abandonment of its franchise. That city is now required to seek special legislation to set up its own transit commission and, if possible, to employ those who are no longer employed as bus drivers by the C.N.R.
Under the provisions of the pension plan there are two types of pensions. One is payable by the C.N.R. in the amount of $25 a month whether or not there has ever been any prior contribution and each of these employees is, of course, entitled to that. This is a maximum of $300 a year. There have been other pension plans set up, however, and that most recently in effect is a contributory one. I should like to refer to the pension plan booklet which is issued to employees coming under the plan and which contains questions and answers with respect to the rules. I have reference to rule 11 and in the booklet there is the following question:
What do I receive if my service is terminated?
This is the answer:
If your service is terminated and you do not qualify for pension benefits, your own contributions will be refunded, together with interest to the date your service is terminated if that date is a year or more from your last entry into service. Your service will not be considered terminated if you are laid off but only when you leave or are discharged.
There is no provision within the pension plan for service which is discontinued and is not replaced. Because the C.N.R. has no comparable service anywhere else in Canada, it is not possible to retain these people in service, and only a very few out of the three groups in Oshawa, Niagara Falls and St. Catharines have been retrained and used elsewhere.
The problem is, of course, that when a municipality is called upon to give a bus service and sets up its own transit commission it does not do this as a profit making venture. Indeed, no municipality would go into the field if there were any way of avoiding it. The ground upon which Canadian National has abandoned these services is that
Canadian National Railways they are uneconomical. Although the municipalities have tried very hard, they have been unable to find anyone who will undertake the service or incorporate a new company and operate the service unless it be done under a subsidy. Because it is not considered a good proposal, all three municipalities in question have in fact set up their own municipal corporations to operate these bus services. They are asked to take over the employees of the C.N.R. who, at a time of great unemployment in southern Ontario, are without employment and without any hope of employment. Some of these people, Mr. Speaker, as of the time they are laid off are only a matter of weeks away from regular retirement on a full pension.
I think everyone in the house knows what the problem is, how are these people to retain the benefits of the pension to which they have contributed for many many years? When they are retired they receive payment of their contributions with interest, of course, but they are not able to take this amount and enter into a brand new pension scheme with their new municipal employers and obtain the same benefits at the same date of retirement.
Representations were made in Oshawa and strenuously in the Niagara area and have been going on for months now. In fact, solicitors on behalf of the unions and solicitors on behalf of the city have attended on the Minister of Transport and the president of Canadian National Railways with requests that some consideration be given in this regard. I raised the matter in the sessional committee and I was told at that time that it was being considered. In fact it had been considered on two prior occasions and both times the portability element was rejected.
At this time there is only a matter of a few weeks remaining in which some action may be taken in order that the pension portion paid by C.N.R. into the fund or at least credited as a bookkeeping entry shall be transferred to a new pension scheme to be operated by the municipality. If not, Mr. Speaker, the result will be that another set of taxpayers, the ratepayers in the communities of St. Catharines and Niagara Falls, will themselves through their taxes be required to subsidize the new pension scheme. This means, of course, that the subsidy principle which Canada has adopted and which we are furthering in this bill, whereby the cost of C.N.R. services across the country is borne by all Canadians, will have been breached for there will be a shifting from all Canadians to individual Canadians in a particular limited area. The position taken by the union, and I respectfully suggest to the house it was a proper one, is that the

Canadian National Railways amounts paid in on behalf of the employer, the Canadian National, are amounts which were in effect fringe benefits to the employees, and having been paid in they are part of the wages to which those employees were entitled.
The minister said in his budget speech that he approved of the principle of portability. I ask the minister to consider that here is perhaps the first place within the government service that portability might be applied. There is, Mr. Speaker, little more that I can say in respect of this. These requests have been taken to the Minister of Transport, to the house, to the committee and to the president of Canadian National. This is a matter which applies to a limited number of people and which has worked a very great injustice. It will further work a great injustice upon these people in the community who may now have to take on these former employees in a new service. I ask the Minister of Finance to consider the appropriateness of this subject since he, and the right hon. gentleman who shares his seat, have already taken a position in respect of other pensions, and about getting rid of these other pensions.
Is the fact that the government stood idly by and allowed these 75 people to have their pensions taken from them, some indication of what the government intends in respect of the governor of the Bank of Canada and other senior civil servants, as was reported in this evening's Journal? If so, not only are these railway employees now without jobs in my area to be frightened that all the money they have paid into the pension has gone for nothing, that their contractual rights are disregarded by the government, but other senior civil servants in the service of Canada must also fear whether what they have paid in by way of contribution in the past will be, by this government which has paid lip service to the bill of rights, disregarded in the same way.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising to support the position taken at the beginning of the day on this measure by the hon. member for Laurier. I refer to the disgraceful attitude of the government with respect to Mr. Donald Gordon and the directors of Canadian National who, for nine months and eight days, have been kept in suspense as to whether or not they are to retain their positions.
Yesterday in this house we watched the leader of the government wield the axe. Today, we are discussing a genlteman who has given long and great service to this country, who for nine months and eight days has been kept under suspended sentence, not knowing upon which day the axe 

will strike his neck or whether he may get another reprieve. How anyone can expect the greatest railway on the North American continent to be run well under circumstances of that sort, I cannot understand and neither can any other reasonable person in this country. It is just more evidence, if any more were needed, of the total incapacity of Her Majesty's present ministers to come to any decision on anything except when the Prime Minister gets into one of those hysterical rages and makes a decision, as he so obviously showed yesterday had happened in the case of the governor of the Bank of Canada.
The position on which I rest our case is the position of the hon. member for Laurier. It is this parliament that is sovereign and not the right hon. gentleman. It is this parliament that is in final control of the affairs of this country and not the right hon. gentleman and his messenger boy colleagues. It is this parliament that has a right to know how all these affairs are going to be carried on before money is voted. It is this parliament that has the right, before hundreds of millions of dollars are committed to a company, to know who is going to be the head of that company. As the hon. member for Laurier has said, we only know who will be the head perhaps until Monday. I do not suppose the government will have a cabinet meeting on Sunday and change the head of the railway, although they might. If they act in the way in which they usually act, they will wait until parliament is out of the way before they do this. They will show the respect for parliament which they have shown in every other matter, and which they showed when the Minister of Finance tried to go behind the back of parliament on another occasion about an officer who was responsible not to him or to the government but to parliament, and tried to subvert the rights of parliament.
The president of the Canadian National is in a different category. The president of Canadian National is the head of a crown company, but not an officer of parliament. The government, it is quite true, has the right, under the statute, to appoint the chairman; but we, sir, this sovereign parliament, have the right to know who that chairman is going to be, and whether or not we should give confidence to a government that appoints that kind of chairman before we are asked to vote this kind of money. This is the principle of responsible government. We heard language yesterday in this house, and if we had closed our eyes, it would have sounded like language that was heard before 1939 in the Reichstag.
